support: Open-source content management system maintained by the WordPress contributor community. Hosting and paid services are available from many independent providers.
technology: Server side: PHP with a MySQL or MariaDB database, typically running on Apache or Nginx. Client side: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript rendered in a web browser. WordPress recommends current PHP and MySQL or MariaDB versions; check its requirements page before installing.
capabilities: Supports thousands of third-party themes and plugins.
Includes a block-based editor and customizable templates for posts and pages.
Supports custom post types, media management, user roles, and publishing workflows.
Provides a REST API for retrieving and managing site content through other applications.
limitations: The site owner is responsible for keeping WordPress, themes, and plugins updated when self-hosting.
Third-party plugins and themes can introduce security vulnerabilities or compatibility problems if they are poorly maintained.
A large number of plugins or poorly optimized themes can make a site harder to maintain and may affect performance.
The quality and cost of hosting can affect site speed, reliability, and maintenance requirements.

example.name: TechCrunch
example.verificationSource: The site's public WordPress REST API is available at https://techcrunch.com/wp-json.

support: Open-source content management system developed by the Drupal community and supported by the Drupal Association, a nonprofit organization that supports the project.
technology: Server side: PHP with a supported database such as MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQLite. It runs on web servers such as Apache or Nginx. Client side: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript displayed in a web browser.
capabilities: Uses modules to add functionality and themes to control website appearance.
Supports structured content types, custom fields, media, taxonomy, and detailed user permissions.
Includes tools for content moderation, translation, workflows, and complex content management.
Includes a JSON:API module that exposes content entities through a standardized API.
limitations: Its extensive configuration options can make it more difficult for beginners to learn than simpler website builders.
Building and maintaining a complex Drupal site may require PHP and Drupal development experience.
The hosting environment must meet Drupal's PHP, database, and web-server requirements.
Contributed modules and customizations need to be checked for compatibility when Drupal is updated.

example.name: HEC Montréal
example.verificationSource: Drupal's case study describes HEC Montréal's website as being built on Drupal: https://new.drupal.org/case-study/modernizing-a-leading-business-schools-website

support: Open-source content management system maintained by the Joomla community, with project support from Open Source Matters, Inc.
technology: Server side: PHP with a supported database such as MySQL, MariaDB, or PostgreSQL. It can run on Apache, Nginx, or Microsoft IIS. Client side: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript displayed in a web browser.
capabilities: Supports templates for changing the design and layout of a website.
Supports extensions, including components, modules, and plugins, to add functionality.
Includes multilingual content features, menus, user access levels, and custom fields.
Provides web services and API functionality for integrations with other applications.
limitations: Users need compatible PHP hosting and a supported database, so it is not a fully hosted, maintenance-free service by default.
Some advanced features require installing and configuring third-party extensions.
Extension and template compatibility should be checked before major Joomla upgrades.
Its administration and extension system can take time for new users to learn.

example.name: Vokoloko
example.verificationSource: The official Joomla Showcase identifies Vokoloko as a Joomla 6.x site: https://showcase.joomla.org/browse-sites/25883.html

support: Open-source publishing platform developed by the nonprofit Ghost Foundation. Users can host it themselves or pay for the managed Ghost(Pro) hosting service.
technology: Server side: Node.js with MySQL as the officially recommended production database, commonly running on Nginx. Client side: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Ghost themes use Handlebars, and its APIs exchange JSON data.
capabilities: Provides a publishing editor for creating posts, pages, and newsletters.
Supports custom themes and templates using Handlebars.
Includes built-in member accounts, paid subscriptions, and newsletter publishing features.
Provides Content and Admin APIs, webhooks, and integrations for connecting external services.
limitations: It is primarily designed for publishing, blogging, and membership-based publications rather than being a general-purpose CMS for every type of website.
It does not use a traditional WordPress-style plugin system; additional features are usually connected through integrations, code injection, themes, or APIs.
Self-hosting requires server administration, updates, backups, and maintenance of the supported software stack.
The officially recommended self-hosted production stack is relatively specific, so using a different database or server setup may be unsupported.

example.name: The Browser
example.verificationSource: Ghost features The Browser in its official customer and publication showcases: https://explore.ghost.org/p/the-browser

support: Proprietary, subscription-based hosted commerce platform developed and operated by Shopify Inc. Shopify manages the core hosting and commerce infrastructure.
technology: Hosted server and database infrastructure are managed by Shopify rather than selected by the store owner. Storefront themes use Liquid, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JSON configuration/templates. Developers can connect to Shopify through its APIs and app platform.
capabilities: Provides tools for managing products, inventory, orders, customers, payments, and online stores.
Supports customizable storefront themes, reusable sections, blocks, and templates.
Supports third-party apps and integrations for adding store features.
Provides APIs for custom applications, integrations, and headless storefront development.
Includes commerce features such as shopping carts, checkout, and sales-channel integrations.
limitations: It is a paid proprietary service, with subscription and potentially additional app or transaction costs.
The platform's backend hosting and database are managed by Shopify, so store owners have less server-level control than with self-hosted CMS software.
Some checkout customization and API access depend on the Shopify plan being used.
It is primarily designed for online commerce and may be less suitable for sites that do not need store functionality.
